content: Liquid paraffin, also referred to as paraffinum liquidum, is a highly refined mineral oil that is utilized in both cosmetics and medical applications. This definition aligns with the British Pharmacopoeia (UK), but the term may have different interpretations in other countries. It is important to distinguish cosmetic or medicinal liquid paraffin from the paraffin (or kerosene) used as a fuel. The term paraffinum perliquidum is sometimes used to describe light liquid paraffin, whereas paraffinum subliquidum may refer to a thicker, more viscous or oily form of mineral oil. Liquid paraffin has limited utility as an occasional laxative. However, it is not suitable for regular use due to several potential adverse effects. It can leak from the anus, causing irritation. It may interfere with the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Additionally, it can be absorbed into the intestinal wall, potentially leading to foreign-body granulomatous reactions. If aspirated into the lungs, it can result in lipoid pneumonia, a serious condition. Liquid paraffin is also used in combination with magnesium as an osmotic laxative, marketed under trade names such as Mil-Par, among others.
